4. After hearing, the learned Subordinate Judge came to the finding, on a consideration of the evidence that Md. Asim acquired valid title to the disputed property on the basis of the dead of exchange-as pleaded in the plaint, but that there was nothing on record to show that the defendant was ever a tenant in respect of the disputed premises. It was further held that the defendant was a trespasser in the disputed premises since February-March, 1950 and as such the suit being filed on 7-6-62 was barred by limitation. It was also found-by the leaned Subordinate Judge that the plaintiff having admitted the defendant to be a tenant in respect of the disputed property, the suit was not maintainable in the absence of a notice under section 111(g) of the Transfer of Property Act, determining the tenancy of the defendant. The learned Subordinate Judge also expressed a doubt as to the title of the plaintiff on the view that no satisfactory evidence had been adduced on the plaintiff's side to prove the passing of the consideration of the kabala, Ext. 1 and observed that the plaintiff had rather purchased a litigation. The suit was dismissed on the aforesaid findings. 

 5. The plaintiffs having preferred an appeal against the said judgment, it was beard by the 1st Court of Additional District Judge who reversed the findings of the Trial Court on the questions of the plaintiff's title, the defendant's acquisition of title by adverse possession and the maintainability of the suit, on a consideration of the evidence on record, and decreed the plaintiff's suit on the findings that the plaintiff had acquired valid title by virtue of the Kabala Ext. 1, that the defendant had entered into the disputed premises in August, 1950 and as such the suit was not barred by limitation, and that the defendant having been found to be a trespasser, there was no question of service of notice under section 111(g) of the Transfer of Property Act. 

 7. On the question of the defendant's plea of adverse possession, the learned. Additional District Judge observed that, in coming to the finding that the suit was barred by limitation, the learned Subordinate Judge relied upon a confused statement of P.W.2 out .of context and held on the basis of the said statement of P.W. 2 that the defendant was in possession of the said property since February-March, 1950. The learned Additional District Judge on a consideration of the said testimony of P.W. 2 was, however, of the view that the aforesaid statement of P.W.2 was based on mere guess rather than on any evidence, that the said statement was a mere hearsay; and that the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge being based upon such hearsay evidence was no sustainable. The learned Additional District Judge also found that P.W. 2 having had no personal knowledge of the state of things existing at the time when the defendant entered into the suit house was not a reliable and trustworthy witness in respect of the said matter. The learned Additional District Judge thereafter proceeded to consider the evidence of P.W.3, the Asst. Librarian of the Dacca University and P.W.4, a member of the Town Committee, who, according to him, were competent and disinterested witnesses relied upon their evidence to come to the finding that the defendant had entered into the disputed premises 516 months after the communal disturbances of 1950 i.e., in August, 1950 and held, on the basis of the said finding, that the suit was not barred by limitation. 

 9. The principal question which was raised in the suit was whether the plaintiff's suit was barred by limitation. According to the plaintiff's case, at the time of the execution of the deed of exchange dated 18-5-60 in favour of Md. Asim, it was represented that the defendant was a tenant at will in occupation of the property under its owner Md, Asim as well as the plaintiff who purchased the disputed property from the said Md. Asim, and that the said owners had taken the defendant to be so until 19-5-62 when the defendant for the first time repudiated the tenancy and asserted adverse possession by filing a written objection in H.R. Case No. 273 of 1961. The defendant in his written statement sought to make out a case that after the partition of the country in 1947 he came to Dacca as a refugee and having found the disputed premises vacant forcibly occupied the same in February, 1948 and since then he had been in occupation adversely to the real owners. The Trial Court came to a finding on the basis of the evidence of Md. Asim, P.W. 2, that the defendant was in possession of the disputed premises, not since, February, 1948 but since February, 1950. The learned Additional District Judge reversed the said finding on the 'view that the evidence of P.W. 2 on the question of defendant's possession of the disputed premises since the disturbances of 1950 was mere hearsay evidence and that P.W.2 was not a reliable witness on this question in view of the fact that he had no personal knowledge of the state of possession in respect of the disputed premises in 1950. The learned Additional District Judge also came to the finding on a consideration of the other evidence on record, that the witnesses examined on behalf of the defendant could not be relied upon but P.W.3 and 4 were independent, disinterested and competent witnesses and held, on the basis of the testimonies of the said witnesses that the defendant entered into the disputed premises in August, 1950. 

 "I am at Dacca since 1950. I live at 18 Rajani Bose Road, I saw the suit house in 1950. It is two storied building with 2 rooms in ground floor and one in the First floor. I cannot say of any addition or .alteration. I know the plaintiff since 1950. I have friendship with him. He was residing at Gopibagh first lane, At that time he was Income-Tax practitioner. One week after I got the house, I saw the defdt. Before that I did not enquire who was in possession of the house. 

 A month before my exchange, Badaruddin and Manager of Pyari Lal told me that defdt. was house tenant in suit houses. He said that the defdt. was house tenant. in the suit house since 1950 and the Manager told me that the defdt. paid rent for one year and did not pay after one year. I asked for collection papers for that one year but manager could not produce the same. These talks were before the exchange in the house of Pyari Lal. or Badruddin were not present then. Pyari Lal. I did not enquire who was in the house prior to 1950. The defendant entered the house in February or March, 1950." 

 15. It will appear from the above quoted deposition of P.W. 2 that he stated that one week after he got the house, he saw the defendant and before that he did not enquire who was in possession of the house. The deed of exchange on the basis of which the plaintiff got the disputed house was dated 18-5-60. Therefore it is evident that he had no knowledge of defendant's possession of the house before the said date. He stated also that he did not enquire who was in the house prior to 1950 and the statement which was made immediately thereafter to the effect that the defendant entered in the house in February-March, 1950 was obviously on the basis of his knowledge derived from the enquiry. Having regard to the entire evidence as deposed by the witness, we have no manner of doubt that the learned Additional District Judge was correct in taking the view that the reading of the learned Subordinate Judge of the said evidence was out of context and the finding of the Additional District Judge that it was hearsay evidence was on the basis of his appreciation of said testimony and it does not appear that there was any misreading or misrepresentation in the said appreciation of evidence by the learned Additional District Judge. The learned Judges the High Court clearly exceeded their jurisdiction, as conferred upon them section under 100 C.P.C. in interfering with the said finding. 

 16. The learned Additional District Judge also pointed out on a consideration of the evidence that the said witness had no direct knowledge of the state of affairs with regard to the disputed house as existed in 1905 and as such the statement made by him in regard thereto was not reliable. The learned Judges of the High Court do not appear to have adverted to the said finding. Furthermore, the court of appeal below on a consideration of the entire evidence on record held that P.W.3 and 4 were disinterested competent and reliable witnesses and, relying upon the depositions of the said witnesses, came to the definite finding that the defendant had entered into the disputed premises for the first time in August, 1950. The learned Judges of the High Court do not appear to have noticed the said finding at all. From the judgment under appeal it appears that the argument of the learned advocate of the appellant before the High Court centred round the evidence of P.W.2 only and the finding of the learned Additional District Judge on the basis of the other evidence on record, particularly, the evidence of P.W.3 and P.W.4, was not referred to at all. The learned Judges of the High Court should have noticed that, the decision of the learned Additional District Judge that the Plaintiff's suit was rot barred by limitation, was not only based en his reading of the evidence of P.W.2 as hearsay evidence, but also on his findings that P.W.2 was not a reliable witness and that the entry of the defendant into the disputed premises had been proved by the evidence of P.W.3 and P.W.4 who were held to be competent and disinterested witnesses, to have been within 12 years from the date of the suit. The High Court seems to have acted clearly in excess of jurisdiction in setting aside the judgment of the lower appellate Court and dismissing the suit without reversing the relevant findings of the lower appellate Court. 

 18. Before parting with this case, it is necessary to notice the observation made by the High Court on the question of limitation. The High Court appears to have observed that the case is governed by Article 142 of the Limitation Act and that the plaintiff having failed to show by positive evidence that he was in possession within 12 years from the date of the suit, the suit was barred by limitation. In the instant case the plaint did not make out a case of prior possession of the plaintiffs predecessor and his subsequent dispossession by the defendant: The plaintiff's case, on the other hand, is that the defendant was found to be in possession as a tenant, who subsequently asserted hostile title and claimed adverse possession. According to the plaint, it was a case precisely under Article 144 Sand not under. Article 142. The defendant, on the other hand, pleaded that he was a refugee from India and having found the disputed premises vacant he entered into the suit premises, although he used the expression "forcibly occupied". The issue as to the limitation as framed was whether the suit was barred by limitation and adverse possession and it also indicates that the suit was generally understood to be one under Article 144, rather than under Article 142. In any view of the matter, it was nobody's case that anybody other than the plaintiff's predecessor, who was the rightful owner of the property, was in possession at the time when the possession of the defendant commenced. The question whether the case is governed by Article 142 or by Article 144 is academic, if the finding of the Court of appeal below that the defendant entered into the house in August, 1950 remains unreversed.
